the inspiral and ring down phases of coalescing BBHs are detectable to large distances by ground-based interferometers, and that the merger phase can be detected with moderate SNR and modest accuracy by a noise monitoring algorithm, and can be searched for with high accuracy using numerical relativity templates.

the number of BBH coalecences detectable by initial interferometers could be up to ∼1000 (with ∼2000 mergers detectable by advanced interferometers), and that the number detectable by LISA could be up to 104 (with ∼105 detectable by the Einstein In Space detector).
The main takeaway from our work is that

ground-based interferometers can be expected to find many BBHs in their first few years of operation, and that LISA can be expected to do a very thorough study of the high mass BBHs in our local universe, and perhaps of BBHs at high redshift.
ground-based interferometers will have a rich harvest of BBHs to study, with the potential for significant scientific advances.
